Summary:
Data source overview: The paper “To Trust Or Not To Trust A Classifier” introduces the Trust-Score, a post-hoc metric that estimates whether a classifier’s predicted label is likely to be correct. It filters training points to high-density subsets for every class and compares the test point’s distance to the predicted-class subset with the distance to the nearest alternative class subset. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that high Trust-Scores correlate with agreement with the Bayes-optimal classifier, derive finite-sample rates even on manifold-structured data, and demonstrate across many datasets that Trust-Score outperforms the model’s own confidence at identifying both trustworthy and suspicious predictions.

Inference strategy justification: Interventions are not explicitly prescribed for AI safety, so moderate inference (confidence edges = 2) is used to convert the demonstrated metric into concrete safety actions such as human-in-the-loop routing and distribution-shift monitoring.

Extraction completeness explanation: All main causal chains—from the top-level risk of harmful mispredictions, through calibration failures, theoretical insights about density proximity, the Trust-Score design and implementation mechanisms, empirical/theoretical validation, to three actionable deployment-phase interventions—are captured. Nodes are de-duplicated and interconnected; no isolated nodes remain.

Key limitations: 1) Paper focuses on classification, so interventions may not generalise to generative models. 2) High-dimensional limits of Trust-Score remain an open problem; this is noted but not fully captured as a separate risk node. 3) Confidence values assigned heuristically.
